source.title: MACPO: Weak-to-Strong Alignment via Multi-Agent Contrastive Preference Optimization
source.authors: Yougang Lyu; Lingyong Yan; Zi-Han Wang; Da-Wei Yin; P. Ren; M. de Rijke; Zhao-Chun Ren

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper runs a Naive SFT baseline that fine-tunes the strong student on weak-teacher labels, the direct weak-to-strong intervention, and reports outcomes. MACPO adds a different iterative preference-optimization method.
record.gate_note: The study does not calculate PGR or report a directly comparable weak-supervisor score for the Naive SFT student. It reports alignment scores from a third-party reward model, plus GPT-4 and human pairwise judgments. The GPT-4 and human results below are only for MACPO versus weak-to-strong baselines. Claims about collapse describe behavior under iterative self-alignment or ablation training, not spontaneous failure under distribution shift or shared errors.
record.test_reason: The study runs the Burns-style weak-to-strong setup (7–8B teachers trained on gold labels, Llama2-70b student trained on their labels) for generative helpfulness/harmlessness alignment. It compares a new training method (MACPO) and an adapted confidence loss against Naive SFT on the weak labels, which bears on V2. Its measure is a third-party reward model plus GPT-4 and human pairwise judgments, not PGR, so it is T2 rather than T1. Table 7 also gives one direct weak-teacher vs SFT-student comparison bearing on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct: MACPO improves alignment of both strong students and weak teachers, and more weak teachers allow more improving iterations. The authors also attribute Naive SFT and Confident loss's weaker results to ignoring negative behaviour, and claim MACPO avoids the collapse seen in self-alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The direct Naive SFT baseline uses weak-label supervised fine-tuning. MACPO instead initializes from weak labels and then iteratively trains agents with DPO-style contrastive preference pairs, mutual positive-behavior augmentation, and constructed negative behaviors.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with the number of weak teachers and iteration count; removing positive augmentation, hard-negative construction, or iterative teacher updates reduces performance. Replacing perplexity filtering with random sampling also lowers scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Weak teachers trained by DPO on the strong student's outputs improve across iterations and exceed the best baseline strong students (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak models trained on outputs of a weakly-supervised strong student improve (reverse/mutual weak-to-strong transfer).

fits_no_version.finding: Self-alignment baselines (SPIN, Self-rewarding) degrade after iteration 1–2 in the weak-to-strong setting (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative self-training of a weakly-initialized strong student collapses without outside positive examples.

record.problems: PGR is not reported, and the Naive SFT student is not directly compared with its weak supervisor. The principal automatic results use a third-party reward model; several sweeps and ablations are only shown in figures without extracted numeric values. GPT-4 and human pairwise evaluations use 100 sampled test instances per dataset.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: Table 2 comparisons of MACPO with RLAIF, RLCD, SPIN, and Self-rewarding; these compare the paper's new method with methods outside the weak-to-strong baseline claim. Table 3 comparisons with RLCD and Self-rewarding are likewise omitted. Table 6 MT-Bench scores and Table 7 label perplexity/reward diagnostics are not direct tests of the listed versions. Figure 3 weak-teacher trajectories are not strong-student PGR results.

untested.parts: PGR is never computed and there is no strong ceiling (student trained on gold labels). The weak-teacher vs Naive SFT comparison exists only in Table 7 (100 helpfulness questions) and figure-only Fig. 3 initial points.

No sweep of student or supervisor size. There are three datasets, but nothing analyses how weak-to-strong gain varies with task or what predicts it. No chess or reward-modelling tasks, no representation analysis.
No test of exploitation of unchecked supervisor errors, distribution shift, or shared weak/strong errors.

missing.what: Reward of labels from initialized weak teachers (Llama2-7b 42.31, Mistral-7b 42.63, Llama3-8b 42.94) vs 70B student 37.96: the only direct weak-vs-student comparison
Weak-teacher initialization reward points vs student (figure only)
MT-Bench out-of-domain scores: Naive SFT 2.11, Confident loss 2.23, MACPO 4.63

record.verdict_notes: Weak-to-strong here is generative alignment scored by an OpenAssistant Pythia-6.9B reward model. There is no ceiling model and no PGR. The confident-loss baseline is a data-pooling adaptation, not the original loss. GPT-4 and human evaluations use 100 instances, with MACPO checkpoints picked by highest reward. I reassigned the teacher-count rows from V3 to V2 (ensembling supervisors) and unlinked the own-method ablations. The V1 verdict rests on Table 7 text, which is not in the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Although Naive SFT trains Llama2-70b-base on weak labels, the paper does not compare that student's result directly with the weak supervisor or calculate PGR.
It compares MACPO and its iterations with Naive SFT using alignment scores, but does not calculate PGR; results are on the reported helpfulness and harmlessness settings.
It varies the number of weak teachers and evaluates multiple alignment datasets and weak-teacher backbones. It does not sweep strong-student size or analyze representations as predictors.
No test of exploiting what a weak supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, or shared weak/strong errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student necessarily beating its supervisor are tested or derived.
No vision or other non-language modality experiment.

relationships.condition: MACPO (3 weak teachers) vs Naive SFT on HH-Helpful, HH-Harmless, PKU-SafeRLHF; reward model, GPT-4 and human judgments
relationships.reason: MACPO iter2–3 exceeds Naive SFT by 5–31 reward points (R4,R5,R9,R10,R14,R15,R19,R20). It wins 76–91% of GPT-4 and human pairwise comparisons against Naive SFT and Confident loss (R45–R53).
relationships.display_finding: MACPO iterations 2–3 exceeded naive SFT by 5–31 reward points and won 76–91% of GPT-4 and human comparisons against naive SFT and Confident loss.

source_check.condition: MACPO (3 weak teachers) vs Naive SFT on HH-Helpful, HH-Harmless, PKU-SafeRLHF; reward model, GPT-4 and human judgments
source_check.reason: R4–R5, R9–R10 and R14–R15 show clear reward gains; R45–R50 show GPT-4 wins. Correct the reason: iterations 2–3 gain 11.06–31.51 reward points; human wins against Confident loss include 69%, giving a combined 69–91% range. Human comparison against Naive SFT is not reported.

relation.reason: Directly compares weak-label SFT with training changes and varies weak-teacher count.

tranche.reason: Tests weak-to-strong method gains using iterative contrastive preference optimization and generative alignment judgments, differing from the original method and measures.

source_check.notes: PGR and a strong ceiling are not reported; V2 evidence uses reward and pairwise-judgment gains. The authors' conclusion paraphrase matches the text; highest-reward checkpoint selection applies to GPT-4 evaluation.

statements.correction: Table 1: MACPO iterations 2–3 minus Naive SFT across the three datasets = 11.06–31.51 reward points, calculated from reported scores; HH-Helpful iteration 2 = 69.08 versus 38.30. Table 2: GPT-4 wins versus Naive SFT and Confident loss = 76–89%. Table 3: human wins versus Confident loss = 91%, 69%, 90%; combined range = 69–91%. Human comparison against Naive SFT not reported.
statements.problem: The reward-gain range is inaccurate, and the combined judge range omits the 69% human win rate on HH-Harmless.

statements.correction: Appendix C: generation adaptation pools weak-teacher and strong-student predictions into one training dataset. Table 1, Confident loss versus Naive SFT: HH-Helpful 37.09/38.30; HH-Harmless 59.29/58.49; PKU-SafeRLHF 50.83/51.44; average 49.07/49.41. Student = Llama2-70b-base; metric = reward score.
statements.problem: The cited MACPO rows do not test Burns' original auxiliary loss or report PGR, and their student is 70B rather than at most 14B.

statements.correction: Section 6.2 and Figure 2: one-teacher MACPO degrades after iteration 2 across all datasets; increasing teacher count to three improves alignment and permits more improving iterations.
statements.problem: R21 concerns degradation with one teacher, so it does not demonstrate failure of weak-supervisor ensembling.

statements.correction: Table 1: HH-Harmless MACPO iteration 1 = 59.20 versus Naive SFT 58.49; iterations 2 and 3 = 69.55 and 70.25. Section 6.2: one-teacher MACPO degrades after iteration 2 across all datasets.
statements.problem: The cited rows support a small first-iteration gain or later single-teacher degradation, not a general conclusion that MACPO preference optimization adds little.

reader_labels.reason: Some changes are small, and ablations or random sampling of weak labels reduce performance; the paper does not establish that every training change improves every condition (R8, R15, R27-R44).
